# `Ui.Cli`

[Back to stdlib index](../stdlib.md)

Ipe.Ui.Cli — the Cli shape's line-oriented view surface.

A `Lines msg` value is a structured, line-scoped view: a stack of styled
text lines. It is distinct from both the web `Element msg` and the Tui
`Screen msg`, so putting a web builder or a 2D cell-grid builder into a
`Lines` view is a compile-time type error (IPE-T0001), never a silent drop.

The builders take this module's OWN `Attribute msg`, interned `CliAttr`,
which exposes only honestly line-scoped styles: bold, underline, dim,
reverse, and terminal-palette foreground/background colour. There is no
2D geometry here — no cell spacing, no padding-in-cells, no vertical or
grid alignment — because a line-oriented surface cannot honour them; those
attributes are simply absent from the type rather than quietly discarded.

`text` is the plain-string escape hatch: `Cli.text s` renders `s` as one
line. `Cli.tea`'s `view` field returns `Lines msg`, so `text` is the bridge
for a view that only wants to emit a plain string.

## How a `Lines msg` view reaches the terminal

`Cli.tea` decides its output surface once, at startup, from the gathered
terminal facts (whether stdout is a TTY, whether stdin is a TTY and
echoing, whether they are the same terminal) — never per frame, and never
by re-reading those facts mid run.

On an interactive, echoing terminal, each render writes its lines
separated by a newline and leaves the LAST line open (no trailing
newline), so the user types after the prompt. Before the next frame, an
already-open line is closed with a newline first; a newline-terminated
stdin line closes it too. On `System.exit` or Ctrl-C, an open line is
closed with a trailing newline before the process ends.

Anywhere else (a pipe, a file, a non-echoing or different-terminal
stdin), every line is followed by a newline, full stop: no escape
sequences, no open prompt line, no padding, no clipping. A view of zero
lines writes nothing. Output is then a deterministic function of the
update/view sequence, so a script reading the piped output always sees
the same bytes for the same run.

A styled line's text is wrapped in its SGR open code and a single reset
(`bg` paints only the line's own text, never the rest of the row);
`TERM=dumb` and a piped/file surface both write no styling at all.
`NO_COLOR` drops `color`/`bg` only — bold, underline, dim, and reverse all
survive, since the NO_COLOR convention governs colour, not text
attributes.

Divergences from a naive line-by-line reading, stated here rather than
left silent:

  * A write the program makes outside its view (`Io.print`, stderr) is
    not tracked by the open-line bookkeeping; on the interactive surface
    it may land after an already-open prompt line. A piped/file surface
    is unaffected, since every frame there is newline-closed immediately.
  * A stdin line over the runtime's length limit is dropped, never
    delivered to `Sub.onLine`.
  * A terminal narrower than a line soft-wraps it; the runtime never
    clips program output to fit a width.
  * A styled background colour paints only the text's own cells, never
    the rest of the terminal row.

## `none`

```ipe
none : Lines msg
```

An empty view — renders nothing.

## `text`

```ipe
text : String -> Lines msg
```

`text str` — render `str` verbatim as a single line, no styling.

## `line`

```ipe
line : List (Attribute msg) -> String -> Lines msg
```

`line attrs str` — one styled line: `str` under the line-scoped `attrs`.

## `lines`

```ipe
lines : List (Lines msg) -> Lines msg
```

`lines children` — stack `children` vertically, one under the next.

## `bold`

```ipe
bold : Attribute msg
```

Render a line's text in bold.

## `underline`

```ipe
underline : Attribute msg
```

Render a line's text underlined.

## `dim`

```ipe
dim : Attribute msg
```

Render a line's text dim (faint).

## `reverse`

```ipe
reverse : Attribute msg
```

Render a line's text in reverse video (swap foreground and background).

## `color`

```ipe
color : AnsiColor -> Attribute msg
```

`color c` — the foreground (text) colour, from the terminal palette.

## `bg`

```ipe
bg : AnsiColor -> Attribute msg
```

`bg c` — the background colour, from the terminal palette.
